column2: With business on his mind, Zhou Shaotang woke after only a little sleep at home and hurried to Yang’s house. Clerk Yang was just going out. “Where are you off to?” “I thought I would visit a friend on City God Hill…” “Do not go.” Zhou interrupted him before he could finish. “I have something urgent to discuss with you.” They held their private conference at Yang’s house. Zhou gave a detailed account of the previous night and asked for his opinion. “Let him sell his own land. Why did Yueru say Tang Zishao could not appear in the transaction himself?” “Exactly! I forgot to ask her that.” “Leave that aside for now. What should we do about Magistrate Ma?” “That is precisely what I came to discuss. Yueru has it all nicely worked out: she hopes we shall first report that the takeover went smoothly. Then Tang will be free of all responsibility. But if we wait until he has raised the silver before submitting the report, will we not hold things up? I do have an idea, though.” Zhou suddenly asked, “Do you know anyone who could arrange a substantial loan?” “Money is tight at present. How much do you want to borrow?” “It is not for me. I want Tang to raise a loan against his West Lake fields. Let us get the money into our hands first, however much it is.” Yang thought for some time. “That means putting the land in pledge. Taking land in pledge is less attractive than buying it outright. There are not many people willing to do it, and the formalities are troublesome. It cannot be settled in two or three days.”

Zhou looked crestfallen. “Then it seems our cooked duck may fly away after all.” “Not necessarily. If we can trust him, we might give him some leeway first.” “The trouble is that we cannot trust him. Think of it: he was willing to let his concubine entertain me…” Zhou realized he had let out a secret, but it was too late to call back his words. Yang smiled. “Well! The tower nearest the water catches the moon first. Have you been to bed with Yueru?” “No, no!” Zhou hastened to explain. “Only kissed her lips and felt her breasts. In any case, Tang must be up to something. We shall certainly be taken in if we trust him too readily.” “I see. Let me think.” Yang, after all, knew more about official procedure. He proposed a course that would leave them room to advance or retreat: Ma Fengshi should first submit a report stating that there were still doubtful points in the accounts, that they were being investigated, and that permission was requested to defer closing the case. “Once Tang sees a report that leaves the matter open, he will know he cannot get away and will hurry to find a solution. If he really tries to evade payment, we shall disclose every one of his irregularities. We may gain nothing ourselves, but at least Magistrate Ma will have carried out his commission creditably.” “Excellent! That is the way.” Zhou added, “When we go to Gongji Pawnshop together, let us tell Tang outright that Magistrate Ma has already decided. We should lose no time. You had better inform him now.”

“He is not at home. He has gone to stand in attendance at the governor’s yamen at Meihuabei.” The governor held official audiences on days ending in three or eight. Following the provincial treasurer, the judicial commissioner and the circuit intendants holding substantive posts or special commissions, expectant county magistrates and subordinate officials would go to stand in attendance outside the governor’s yamen. This was a show of respect intended to win favour and strengthen the impression they made. For minor officials awaiting appointments, it was the surest road to advancement. Sometimes, while discussing business with the senior officials, the governor would need someone for a commission. A treasurer, commissioner or intendant entitled to recommend a candidate might remember a suitable man he had just seen. Such unexpected opportunities were by no means rare. “What time did you arrange to meet Tang?” “There is plenty of time yet,” Zhou said. “Let us have a pot of tea at a teashop first.” “No need to go out. I have some good Lu’an tea. I shall brew you a pot.” Yang made the tea and brought out two plates of dry pastries. They ate and chatted. When Yang asked about Yueru, Zhou grew animated at once. He concealed nothing and gave a wealth of description.

Yang listened with relish. “If you had the chance, would Yueru be willing to go to bed with you?” “I am sure she would. In fact, last night I could have had her if I had been bold enough.” “You were afraid Tang would catch you in the act and make you sign a confession?” “Exactly. This business concerns all three of us. I could not do anything so foolish and drag my friends into trouble.” “Shaotang, you would not put a pretty woman before your friends. That shows what a good friend you are. But tell me: do you want to sleep with Yueru or not?” “I do, but there is no opportunity.” “I shall make one for you. When we go to Gongji, I shall keep Tang occupied. You can go straight upstairs to Yueru. I guarantee that no one will catch you together.” “No need, no need!” Even if he could enjoy himself so easily, Zhou reflected, he would still have to consider the hold this would give Yang over him. He must never do anything so foolish. He therefore added, “Thank you for your kindness, but I am still not brave enough. Thank you, all the same.” Yang had genuinely meant to help him attain his desire. Seeing him so determined, however, he could hardly press the matter. He merely smiled.

“You have reminded me of something, though. I could still call on Yueru and ask her that question you raised.” “Then I am to go to Gongji alone?” “Yes. You go ahead. I shall follow as soon as I have asked her.” “Should I tell Tang about it?” Yang asked. “No need. Just say I shall be along shortly.” Towards noon they reached the lane beside Gongji Pawnshop and parted for the moment. Zhou went to Tang’s house and knocked. After a long wait without an answer, he turned away in disappointment. As he did so, he saw Yueru approaching at an unhurried pace, her maid behind her with a market basket on her arm. Mistress and maid had just returned from buying food. “What good timing!” Zhou said. “A moment later for you, or a moment earlier for me, and we should have missed each other.” “You have come at just the right time too, Mr Zhou. I was lucky enough to find fresh mushrooms today. Stay for lunch.” “No, no! Clerk Yang is waiting for me at Gongji.” “Then invite him too.” “We shall see in a moment. Sister-in-Law, let me sit with you first. There is something I want to ask.” The maid had already opened the door. They went in and sat in the reception room. Yueru invited him upstairs, but he declined. He meant to stay only long enough for a few words and felt there was no need to put her to any trouble.

“Sister-in-Law, yesterday you said Old Tang could not appear in person to sell the West Lake fields. Why is that?” Yueru had not expected this question. She was taken aback, and it also reminded her of something else, making her still more uneasy. Zhou sensed something strange in her reaction, and suspicions began to cloud his mind. “Please sit for a moment, Mr Zhou. I have suddenly remembered an instruction I must give first.” She called, “A’cui! A’cui! What are you doing? We have a guest, and you have not even made tea.” “I am in the kitchen boiling water,” A’cui answered loudly, coming out. “Go to the bridge and tell him we have a guest. Ask him to come this afternoon instead.” A’cui stared blankly. For the moment she could not think whom she was to inform at the bridge. “Go on!” “Yes, yes,” she faltered. “Whom am I to tell?” “Did we not just go there and ask the owner to come at once?” “Oh, yes! The furniture shop, the furniture shop.” She turned and left. “What a fool!” Yueru muttered. Turning back, she said, “Forgive me, Mr Zhou. I did not quite catch your question.”

“Why can Old Tang not show himself when selling the land?” Yueru’s real reason was that a sudden sale by Tang would start rumours and suspicions. Was he leaving Hangzhou? Was he returning to his old home in Anhui? Such talk would interfere with their plans to slip away, which was why he could not appear himself. Naturally, she now gave a different answer. “Since Gongji has been taken into official custody, some people probably know that our master has a shortfall in his accounts. Even those who do not will ask why he is selling land. Once they learn that he needs the money to make good a deficit, they are bound to force down the price. It is better for him to keep out of sight.” The reason was persuasive, and her tone composed. Zhou’s suspicions vanished. “You really do think of everything, Sister-in-Law.” He stood up. “That was all I wanted to ask. Now I understand, I must go.” He had not gone far towards Gongji when he met A’cui coming back, her long plait swinging as she walked with a sway. “Going home, Mr Zhou?” she greeted him. “No, I am going to Gongji.” “Look.” She turned and pointed. “Straight along here, over a little bridge, and you are at Gongji’s back entrance.” Zhou had intended to leave the lane, reach the main street and enter by the front. A shortcut to the rear would save him some effort. “Thank you,” he said with a smile. “So there is a back entrance too.” “It saves a good deal of walking.” She added politely, “Do come and see us often, Mr Zhou, whenever you have time.”

Her attentiveness reminded Zhou of something. As a guest at Tang’s house the previous night, he should have given the servants a tip. “A’cui, wait a moment,” he called. Reaching inside his fur-lined robe, he felt among several pieces of silver in a pocket and chose one of a suitable size, weighing perhaps three or four tenths of a tael. He held it out. “What is this for, Mr Zhou?” “For you. I forgot when I left yesterday.” “No, no!” “You must not refuse.” He put on a stern face. “That would be bad manners.” A’cui smiled, thanked him and went happily on her way, swinging her plait. Zhou followed her directions. Sure enough, he came to a little stone bridge. Beside it stood a second-hand shop, with old wooden furniture piled out into the roadway. Something struck him. He stopped and looked carefully around but could see no furniture shop. Could Yueru have meant this second-hand dealer? He went over to ask. “Excuse me, where is the furniture shop around here?” “I have no idea,” the dealer answered in surprise. “I have never heard of one. Who told you that? Someone is sending you on a fool’s errand.” “It was…” Suspicion rose again, and Zhou resolved to get to the bottom of it. “Perhaps I heard wrongly. At Master Tang’s house—the pawnbroker from Gongji—they said there was a furniture shop here and they wanted to buy some furniture from you.” “Either you heard wrongly or you have got it wrong. They want to sell furniture, not buy it. They asked me to look it over and give them a price.” “Why does she want to…” Zhou broke off. He had meddled quite enough already. More questions would arouse suspicion. He smiled, said, “My mistake,” and strode away.

At Gongji he found Tang looking very unhappy, with an expression compounded of vexation and anxiety. Clearly Yang had told him what they had decided to do. Nevertheless, Tang greeted Zhou with a show of warmth and respect, coming forward to clasp his hand. “My dear elder brother, you must help me, whatever happens.” “What is it?” Zhou asked, pretending ignorance as he sat down. He exchanged a glance with Yang, warning him to be cautious. “Old Yang tells me Magistrate Ma intends to submit a report saying my accounts are not clear.” Tang spoke urgently. “How can he put that in an official report?” “What does it matter? Put the accounts in order, and that will be the end of it.” “That is not how it works. It is like leaving a footprint. With such a record against me at the yamen, it will be difficult for me to do anything or hold up my head afterwards.” “Then what do you want?” “Why, Mr Zhou!” Tang pointed at him. “Did you not promise to ask Magistrate Ma to hold the matter back for a while?” “Only for a day or half a day,” Yang put in. “What can I do in a day or two? Money is so tight now.” “All right, I understand,” Zhou said. “Old Tang, a man doing business must know how to behave. If you do not, others cannot help you even if they wish to. Let us do this: find a way as quickly as you can, while Old Yang and I plead with Magistrate Ma for you. We shall meet again this evening.” He had already risen to leave.

“No hurry, no hurry!” Tang said hastily. “I have sent someone to order dishes. Have lunch before you go.” “We shall not stay for lunch.” A sudden idea occurred to Zhou, and he deliberately gave Tang a fright. “To tell the truth, someone has been watching us since we came here. We had better leave at once.” This alarmed not only Tang but Yang, whose face changed colour. “Whose men?” he asked quietly. “Where are they?” “Men from the Hangzhou prefecture. You will see when you go out.” Zhou started for the door, with Yang close behind. “Wait a moment, both of you!” Tang hurried after them. “How shall we meet this evening?” “I shall come to see you.” “Very well. I shall await your visit.” Zhou strode out in front. Once outside Gongji, he kept looking back. Yang asked anxiously, “Where are they?” Zhou burst out laughing. “Forgive me! I have even frightened you. Let us go up City God Hill for yousuobing cakes. I shall tell you everything.”

They climbed City God Hill and sat down in the tavern next to Yaoshi. Its owner, surnamed Chen, knew Zhou well and also knew Yang. He rose from his account desk to attend to them himself. “What brings you up City God Hill in such cold weather? A rare pleasure! What would you like?” “We came especially for yousuobing. Any dishes will do, but the wine must be good,” Zhou said. “I have a jar of fine Huadiao, almost all sold. Three jin remain. Will that be enough?” “We shall drink less at noon. That will do.” “Last time I had your ‘one chicken, four ways,’ and it was excellent,” Yang said. “Let us have it again. Make sure the chicken is fat.” “Leave it to me, Mr Yang.” The wine was heated, and they began with ready-made small dishes: sprouted beans, dried fish in tea-seed oil and the like. Zhou now told Yang that nobody had been watching them. He had merely meant to frighten Tang.

“There is something very strange, though. I cannot make out what Yueru is up to.” Once Zhou had described his discovery that the Tangs meant to sell their furniture, Yang reached an immediate conclusion. “Tang is going to take his concubine and run away.” Zhou thought so too. “Where would he go? Surely not back to Huizhou?” “If he fled to Huizhou, they could still bring him back. His only chance is Shanghai. If he hides in the foreign settlements and takes care, he will not be easy to catch. I think he is playing for time. Selling land takes ten days or half a month at the very least. That would give him more than enough time to slip away.” “Yes, yes. Then what should we do?” Yang had no good answer either. They drank in silence for a while. Suddenly he set down his cup, rested both hands on the table and leaned forward. In a low voice he said, “I shall be honest with you. When you joked just now about someone watching us, I was in a terrible state. As the saying goes, do nothing shameful by day and you need not fear a knock at midnight. A windfall can cost a man his life. You cannot force it. Let us give Magistrate Ma a chance to earn some credit. Tell him to report the facts. Tang has brought this on himself; we need not pity him. What do you say?” Zhou considered, then nodded. “I agree. But the amount must be reduced.” “Why?” “Did I not tell you? Mr Hu wants to repay Yueru’s kindness. We had meant to give him a share, but he does not want it. He is making it a present to Yueru. So we cannot report the full amount Tang has embezzled.”

Somehow the words “Mr Hu” reached Chen’s ears. He strolled over to ask for news, and naturally there were sighs and expressions of regret. Zhou and Yang sat beside a window of intricate latticework covered in white paper, with a square of glass set into the middle. Through it they could see an evergreen pine, its lofty crown spreading like a canopy. On fine days in spring and autumn, the space beneath it made an excellent place for tea. Chen pointed. “Under that pine is where Mr Hu and Governor Wang sat the first time they came for tea and wine. Governor Wang mentioned it particularly on a later visit. That was seventeen or eighteen years ago.” “If Governor Wang knew how Mr Hu would end, I doubt he could rest in his grave,” Yang said with deep feeling. “Such a magnificent enterprise, gone just like that! Exactly like General Nian.” “Still, he is much better off than General Nian,” Zhou said. “At least his life is not in danger.” “Even if his life is safe,” Chen added, “what pleasure can there be left in living?” “True.” Yang nodded gravely. “The higher you climb, the harder you fall. Better to take things less to heart.”

They went on talking about Hu until they had eaten and drunk their fill. Only as they walked down the hill together did Zhou return to Tang. “I promised him we would count only twenty-four thousand taels. Tell Magistrate Ma that if he submits a report, that is the figure he should use.” “Very well,” Yang said. “But you ought to explain it all to Mr Hu. We are reducing the amount out of consideration for Tang’s concubine, just as he wished. The three of us are simply following official procedure. Otherwise he may think we have made a fortune out of it. That would be unfair to us.” He added, “Please be sure to tell him that.” Yang spoke so earnestly that Zhou decided to visit Yuanbao Street. Hu was no longer receiving visitors, but his affection for Zhou was different. He had him shown in and asked what had brought him. “I have seen that ‘slender horse’ you spoke of. Only seen her—nothing more,” Zhou said. “Tang’s deficit comes to at least eighty thousand taels. In accordance with your wishes, we have cut it to thirty per cent. Once the report goes in, they will of course have to recover it. Whatever they collect can go towards repaying the government money you owe. It will be of some help.”

Hu’s eyes reddened. “Shaotang, those words alone are enough. Since my troubles began, even my closest friends have come to settle accounts with me. At most they offer to knock something off and let me repay a little less. Not one has said, ‘Never mind that deposit I brought you. Leave it there for now.’ As for helping me raise money, you could say there has been nobody. Only two exceptions: Gu Yingchun, who helped scrape together two or three hundred thousand taels to meet the panic in Shanghai, and you. Gu has benefited from me; we have always helped one another. But you are giving up money you could rightfully earn by your own abilities and diverting it to make good my deficit. A cup of water on a cartload of burning wood, perhaps—too little to save anything. Yet to me these twenty-four thousand taels are more precious than anything else.” “Mr Hu, you must not put it that way. I too benefited from you in the old days.” Zhou went on, “At noon today we were having yousuobing on City God Hill and spoke of your friendship with Governor Wang. If he heard of this disaster, I doubt he could be at peace even in the other world.” The mention of Wang Youling brought back the past and his lost friend. Hu felt still more painfully close to tears. “It has all been one great dream,” he said. “A dream is a dream. In the end one has to wake.” “From ancient times to the present, there can have been only a handful of men who ever dreamed a dream like yours.”

These words encouraged Hu. Suddenly he thought of something that had never occurred to him before: his reputation after death. “I wonder whether storytellers will tell of me one day. And if they do, what will they say? That I brought ruin upon myself, or that my luck failed?” “They certainly will tell your story. Just like General Nian—who has not heard of him?” This reminded Hu of the story of General Nian giving away a concubine. An idea stirred in him. He smiled. “How could I compare with General Nian? Let us leave that aside and talk of family matters, as old friends should. Shaotang, how old are you this year?” “I was born in the Year of the Tiger. Fifty-four.” “And your wife?” “The Year of the Sheep, five years younger. In theory, with a sheep in a tiger’s jaws, my influence ought to harm her. Yet her health is even better than mine.” “You do not look in your fifties at all. I last saw your wife when we were young. I thought you were a little afraid of her then. What about now?” “At our age, what does it matter who fears whom? Besides…” “Why stop there?” Hu asked. Zhou had reached a painful subject and did not wish to speak of it. He shook his head. “It is nothing.”

“There must be a reason. Shaotang, if something is troubling you, why not tell me?” “It is not that. Our only son…” Zhou’s only son had been thirty that year. He worked for a foreign firm in Shanghai and was highly valued by its chief. With maritime restrictions lifted and foreign business flourishing, his prospects had seemed splendid. Then, in the second month, a spring epidemic had carried him off. Mrs Zhou had been beside herself with grief. What Zhou had begun to say was, “Besides, a young husband and wife become companions in old age. With our only son dead, she and I truly have no one but each other.” It was this painful memory that had stopped him. “Had your son married?” Hu asked. “No.” “Why was he still unmarried at thirty?” “He had taken to foreign ways. He said foreigners did not marry until thirty. He also wanted to go abroad with his employer and learn something useful. Marriage would have made that inconvenient, so he kept putting it off. Now that delay has cost us even a grandson.”

“Yes. Of the three offences against filial duty, leaving no heir is the worst,” Hu said. “Has your wife not urged you to take a concubine?” “She has. I told her…” Zhou stopped abruptly. What he had actually said was, “Forget it. If you want discord at home, take a concubine.” As the words reached his lips, he remembered how offensive they might be. First, Madam Luosi was herself a concubine. Second, Hu’s household had its “Twelve Beauties.” Perhaps having so many concubines was part of what had brought him to his present plight. In any event, words that would wound him must not be spoken. Zhou changed his answer. “My wife meant it kindly, but I could not find a suitable woman just then. I could only decline with thanks.” “That is true enough. Finding the right woman is the most important thing. ‘If you want discord at home, take a concubine.’ People always assume this means the principal wife grows jealous. It need not be so at all! Choose badly, and the concubine sees a quiet principal wife whom she can bully. Spoiled by her husband’s favour, she tries to climb over the wife’s head. Then there will be quarrels, however virtuous the wife may be.” Zhou had not expected Hu himself to quote the very saying he had thought too delicate to mention. Yet there was much truth in his words. Madam Luosi was a ready example; Zhou also knew what had happened when Gu Yingchun took a concubine. Both experiences could serve as footnotes to Hu’s argument.
